title: Marks at Riverbank College
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Every year the teachers of Riverbank College, an imaginary school, compare the average marks that pupils receive in four subjects: mathematics, history, science and art. The marks over the last four years show a number of interesting patterns. This passage describes them and offers some possible explanations. It also asks whether the changes are a reason for celebration or for concern, and what the school should do next to improve the results in every subject. The figures are averages for about four hundred pupils in each year, so a small change in the marks of a few pupils is unlikely to have much effect on the pattern.

In mathematics, the average mark has risen each year. Four years ago, it was well below the other subjects, but a new programme of weekly small-group lessons has helped weaker pupils, and the results have climbed steadily since. The head of mathematics says that the greatest improvement is among pupils who once lost confidence in the subject, and that the extra lessons have taught them to ask questions instead of hiding their difficulties.

History has moved in the opposite direction. The average mark was the highest of the four subjects at the beginning of the period, but it has fallen every year since. Teachers suggest several reasons: the course has become longer, the number of lessons has been reduced to make room for other subjects, and many pupils now prefer to read short summaries online instead of whole books. The school is considering restoring the lost lessons.

Science shows no clear change at all. The average mark has stayed at almost the same level for four years, and the differences between one year and the next are too small to be significant. Some teachers regard this stability as a sign of a mature and well-organised course. Others fear that it indicates a lack of fresh ideas, and they have asked for new equipment so that pupils can carry out more experiments for themselves.

Art follows a more unusual pattern. Marks rose sharply during the first two years, after the school opened a new studio and employed a second teacher. Since then, however, they have fallen back to roughly their previous level. The head of art believes that the first rise was due to the novelty of the new facilities, and that the second change took place because the extra teacher left and was not replaced for a full year.

What lessons can be drawn from these four cases? Dr Samira Haddad, an education researcher who has studied the school, says that marks are influenced by many factors and that it is dangerous to explain a change by a single cause. She notes that investment in a subject often leads to quick results, but that the results fade unless the investment is kept up. She recommends that the school watches the trends for several more years before it makes any large decisions.

The school has decided to follow her advice. It will keep the small-group lessons in mathematics, restore some of the lessons in history, and ask the science staff for a plan for improvement. In art, it will recruit a replacement teacher as soon as possible. The headteacher said that the aim is not to have every subject rise at the same speed, but to ensure that no pupil is left behind and that each subject has the support that it needs to flourish. Parents will be sent a short report each term, and a meeting is planned for the spring so that families can ask questions about the results and about the plans for the coming year.
